articles.title: How a Chinese company is using Blue Light to fight mosquitoes, claims 30 kills per second: Scans the area, locks on in 3 milliseconds and...
articles.summary: Tech News News: Mosquitoes kill roughly 700,000 people a year, which makes them the deadliest animal on the planet by a wide margin. Our defences have not changed muc.
articles.body: Mosquitoes kill roughly 700,000 people a year, which makes them the deadliest animal on the planet by a wide margin. Our defences have not changed much in a century: nets, coils, sprays, and a rolled-up newspaper. A startup in Changzhou, in eastern China, thinks the next step is a laser turret that sits on your patio and shoots the insects out of the air.Photon Matrix has opened preorders for its blue laser mosquito air defense system at $1,088, roughly Rs 95,000, after starting mass production in August. The company says the device locks onto a mosquito in three milliseconds and can take down up to 30 of them a second, in complete darkness, without chemicals and without noise. Those are the company's own numbers, and nobody outside the company has verified them yet.How the Photon Matrix laser mosquito killer finds a 2mm target in the darkThe unit scans a flat fan of light across the space in front of it and continuously measures how far away the background is. When something small crosses that plane, the distance reading changes. The system then checks the size, and if it matches a mosquito, between 2mm and 20mm moving slower than a metre per second, an internal galvo mirror points the laser down the same optical path the LiDAR just used and burns the wings. Coverage is a six-metre radius across a 90-degree arc, and a rotating base spins the device for something closer to full coverage. A companion app logs kills, plots a mosquito heat map, sets on-off schedules and, for reasons known only to the marketing team, ranks you on a global leaderboard.The blue laser mosquito zapper's safety case has no independent testing behind itThe obvious question about a laser strong enough to disable an insect is what happens when it misses. Photon Matrix's answer is a background check: the laser fires only when it detects a solid surface within range, and shuts off when it cannot find one. The company says the system has cleared certifications covering people, pets and birds, and that it ignores butterflies and other larger insects. It has also promised to publish more testing and safety data. Until an independent reviewer gets a unit on a table, buyers are taking that on trust, and the comment sections under every video of this thing are full of people asking about eyes.The mosquito laser is a 20-year-old idea that finally shippedThere are two versions. The outdoor blue laser model at $1,088 flashes visibly each time it fires. The indoor infrared model, at $988 or about Rs 87,000, uses a 976nm invisible beam pitched at bedrooms and hotel rooms. Both come with a rotating base, a 12-month warranty and a 20,000mAh power bank good for around four hours off mains. Delivery is quoted at roughly 120 days.The project raised $2.7 million on Indiegogo against a $20,000 target, with over 4,000 backers paying about $630 each, then slipped repeatedly on sensor calibration and safety approvals. The concept itself dates to 2006, when an astrophysicist who worked on Reagan-era missile defence pitched it at a brainstorming session. A prototype turret with a 50-metre range was demonstrated in 2010 and never found a buyer.So the century-old arsenal gets a new entry, and it works out to about a thousand dollars for the privilege of watching mosquitoes fall.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: In 1994, Arthur and Helen Chapman bought a former Black schoolhouse in Maryland; today, its original blackboard remains
articles.summary: US News: Arthur and Helen Chapman bought Lutherville Colored School No. 24 in Maryland in 1994, when the former two-room schoolhouse had already spent decades .
articles.body: Arthur and Helen Chapman bought Lutherville Colored School No. 24 in Maryland in 1994, when the former two-room schoolhouse had already spent decades out of use. They restored the building and turned it into a museum of African American history. One of the classrooms still contains the original blackboard used by students at the school even after two decades.A two-room school for Black childrenThe schoolhouse was constructed around 1908 and opened in 1909 on School Lane in Lutherville, Baltimore County. It was built for Black children during the era of segregated public education and served students in grades one through seven. The building had two classrooms. The first three grades occupied one room, while grades four through seven used the larger room. Students came from Lutherville and nearby communities including Cockeysville, Beaver Dam, Riderwood, Ruxton, Brightside and Bare Hills.The school did not have indoor bathrooms, so students and teachers used an outhouse. Teaching materials were also limited compared with those available at white schools in the county, according to Baltimore Heritage’s historical account.High school was not an option nearbyFor Black students who wanted to continue their education beyond the elementary grades, opportunities were restricted. Baltimore County did not have a public high school for Black students until Carver High School opened in Towson in 1939. Before that, some students had to attend schools in Baltimore City. For families who could not afford transportation or other costs, continuing their education could be difficult. Lutherville Colored School No. 24 eventually closed in 1955, and the building was later used by Baltimore County for storage.The Chapmans bought the abandoned schoolhouseArthur and Helen Chapman purchased the former school from Baltimore County in 1994. The couple had a family connection to the building through Marie E. Jackson, a former student who had lived across the street. The Chapmans spent more than $100,000 restoring the structure, according to the museum’s own account. They dedicated it as a museum in 1996 in Jackson’s honor.The restoration preserved the building as a schoolhouse rather than turning it into a conventional private residence or commercial property. The museum’s collection includes schoolbooks, report cards, oil lamps, furniture and oral histories connected to the school and the surrounding Black community.The original classroom is still thereThe original blackboard and cement foundation survived, and one classroom has been arranged to show how the school looked during its operating years. The Associated Press documented the preserved blackboard when it reported on Maryland’s former segregated schools. Books, desks and other classroom materials are displayed alongside information about the students who attended.The preservation also keeps the school’s place in Baltimore County’s segregated education system visible. After Brown v. Board of Education in 1954, Maryland’s segregated school system began moving toward integration, and Lutherville Colored School No. 24 closed the following year.A schoolhouse that became a museumThe museum has remained connected to the community more than a century after the school opened. Former students and their families have returned for gatherings, while the building has been used to preserve photographs, documents and memories associated with the school. Arthur and Helen Chapman died in 2021. Their son, David Chapman, later took over ownership, while Karen Darden has helped operate the museum and organize events. The former Lutherville Colored School No. 24 remains at its original location, with its classroom and blackboard preserved as part of the museum.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Delhi’s MPD-2047 launched by DDA: From property rules to development norms, 10 key FAQs answered
articles.summary: News News: The Delhi Development Authority (DDA) has launched a set of Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on the Master Plan for Delhi 2047 (MPD-2047), providing .
articles.body: The Delhi Development Authority (DDA) has launched a set of Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on the Master Plan for Delhi 2047 (MPD-2047), providing citizens, property owners, developers and other stakeholders with simplified information on its provisions.The initiative is part of the DDA’s digital outreach efforts following a direction from Delhi Lieutenant Governor Taranjit Singh Sandhu to make the provisions of the new master plan more accessible.MPD-2047 is Delhi’s new long-term land-use and development framework, setting out norms for construction, redevelopment, land pooling, transit-oriented development and other forms of urban growth across the city.It came into force on August 20, 2026, and supersedes MPD-2021. The FAQs cover a wide range of issues, including land use, development control norms, redevelopment, land pooling, transit-oriented development (TOD), High Density Corridors (HDC), Low Density Areas, heritage and in-situ slum rehabilitation.For the real estate sector, the document provides clarity on permissible FAR, minimum plot sizes, redevelopment eligibility, land pooling participation, development potential under TOD and HDC policies, and Transferable Development Rights (TDR).The DDA has also introduced an “MPD-2047 (Feedback)” facility on its citizen services platform, allowing citizens and stakeholders to submit suggestions and feedback related to the master plan.Here are 10 key FAQs from the DDA’s MPD-2047 document, answered by the authority:Q1. Since when will MPD-2047 be applicable?MPD-2047 is in force from the date of its notification in the Official Gazette, i.e., August 20, 2026.Q2. Do all existing developments have to comply with the provisions of MPD-2047 immediately?Plans approved prior to notification of MPD-2047 shall continue as per earlier norms. The new norms shall apply only when additional FAR is availed, wherever applicable, or when a revised plan is sanctioned.Q3. What provisions have been made for redevelopment under different land uses?MPD-2047 allows redevelopment at the plot level with the following provisions:General Eligibility: The minimum plot area for redevelopment is 3,000 sqm for Residential areas and 1,000 sqm. for Commercial, Industrial and Public & Semi-Public (PSP) areas, unless otherwise specified.Residential Areas: Redevelopment provisions have been made for Government and Employer Housing, Cooperative Group Housing Society (CGHS)/DDA Housing.Commercial Areas: Redevelopment is permitted for District Centres, Community Centres, Local Shopping Centres and Convenience Shopping Centres. Standalone cinema sites may also be redeveloped for commercial use.Industrial Areas: Provisions have been made for regeneration of plotted and flatted industrial areas.Public & Semi-Public (PSP) Areas: Redevelopment is permitted at both the scheme level and the individual plot level.Special development areas (Walled City, Walled City Extension, and Karol Bagh) - Heritage-sensitive regeneration and redevelopment under dedicated area-specific schemes is permitted.The detailed mechanism and procedure for the redevelopment process shall be as per the Regulations to be notified.Q4. Is redevelopment allowed on residential plotted development?Only reconstruction shall be allowed on all residential plots as per the prescribed FAR, unless otherwise specified. Redevelopment shall not be allowed.Q5. What is the permissible FAR for group housing?The maximum FAR for Group Housing is 200, with a minimum plot area of 3,000 sq m. The minimum plot area is 2,000 sq m in Lal Dora/Extended Lal Dora areas.Q6. What is the permissible FAR under the TOD Policy?The base FAR shall be 400, subject to payment of TOD charges. The maximum permissible FAR shall be 500, subject to payment of Additional FAR Charges in addition to TOD charges.Q7. Is participation in TOD policy mandatory?No, participation in TOD Policy is voluntary. Plot owners not willing to participate in TOD policy may continue with the existing use as per Master Plan Provisions.Q8. What is the Land Pooling Policy of Delhi?Land Pooling Policy is a new framework for urban development, wherein the private entity/ landowners will play an active role in development of land along with DDA through assembly of land, Town Planning Scheme or through any other models. Land owner/groups of land owners may participate for development of their land parcels as per prescribed norms and regulations.Q9. What percentage of land shall be retained by landowners under the Land Pooling Policy?The Land Use distribution shall be as per the development model of the Land Pooling Scheme. As per the present development model for assembly of land by 10 group of landowner, a maximum of 60% of pooled land in every scheme shall be available to land owners for development and remaining 40% land is to be surrendered to DDA for development of city level commercial & services (Recreational, PSP, Roads & Circulation), and saleable component.Q10. What is Transferable Development Rights (TDR) and where can it be used?Transferable Development Rights (TDR) means an award specifying the extent of unutilised FAR on a plot/land that can be sold or utilised on an alternate site as specified by the Master Plan. Plot from where TDR originates shall be the ‘Generating Site’ and where it is utilised shall be the ‘Receiving Site’.Under MPD-2047, TDR may be generated from conservation/preservation of heritage buildings, regeneration of buildings in the walled city and in-situ slum rehabilitation schemes /projects. The generated TDR may be utilized only in the TDR receiving areas in the city as identified by DDA, from time to time. A dedicated single window portal shall be developed and maintained by DDA to facilitate TDR trading.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: In 1978, Richard Branson bought a bare 74-acre Caribbean island for $180,000; it now shelters more than 140 animal species, including breeding lemurs and giant tortoises
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover how Richard Branson transformed the barren Necker Island into a thriving sanctuary for over 140 animal species, including endangered lemurs and giant tortoises.
articles.body: In 1978, Richard Branson, then 28, paid $180,000 for a small, uninhabited island in the British Virgin Islands. Necker Island had no fresh water source, no buildings and barely any vegetation beyond scrub and cactus. Nearly fifty years after the purchase, and roughly four decades since the resort itself was completed, that same 74-acre island supports a working conservation programme that shelters well over 140 species, several of which now breed there naturally, including lemurs from Madagascar and giant tortoises from the Seychelles.A reluctant purchase becomes a passionBranson has told the story of the purchase many times over the years, and the details rarely change. According to an account he has given describing the negotiation, he first visited the British Virgin Islands on a trip meant to impress a woman he was pursuing at the time, having been offered a free look at the islands by a realtor who did not realise how little money Branson actually had. The asking price for Necker was around six million dollars, far beyond what he could afford at the time, running an eight-year-old record label, so Branson made an opening offer of just $100,000. The seller turned him down at first but came back a year later, still unable to find a buyer, and eventually accepted a revised offer of $180,000. At that point he owned essentially raw land, with no infrastructure, and the sale came with a condition that he build a resort on the site within four years. Turning that bare ground into something worth visiting took nearly a decade and set the pattern for what followed: a slow, deliberate transformation rather than a quick development.Building a home for species with nowhere else to goThe wildlife did not arrive all at once, and it was introduced deliberately. Over the decades since the resort was completed, Branson and his team have deliberately introduced species that were struggling in their native ranges, choosing Necker specifically because its isolation from the mainland makes it easier to protect animals from predators and disease, even though the island itself operates as a small, tightly controlled private resort where guest access to the animals is limited and managed by the conservation team. As Branson explains in a PBS documentary filmed on the island, lemurs have become one of what he calls the island's flagship conservation species, brought in after habitat loss in Madagascar left many of their relatives fighting for survival at home. Giant tortoises, native to the Aldabra atoll in the Seychelles, followed a similar path, arriving as part of a breeding programme rather than as a decorative addition to the grounds. Flamingos, macaws, iguanas and a rotating cast of other species have joined them, each one added with the specific aim of giving vulnerable animals a secure place to establish new populations. That patient approach appears to be paying off in the way conservationists actually measure success, through births rather than just headcounts.A sanctuary that sustains itselfToday, the tortoises in particular have reached a milestone that is rare in captive conservation work, breeding naturally on the island rather than relying on animals shipped in from elsewhere to maintain their numbers. A dedicated wildlife team now manages the island's animal population full time, treating Necker less like a private garden and more like a functioning sanctuary with its own breeding programmes and veterinary oversight. Branson himself has framed it in exactly those terms in his own public comments, describing a personal commitment to protecting disappearing species that has clearly outlasted his initial reasons for buying the place at all. Necker Island remains one of a small number of personal purchases from that era that developed decades later into an active conservation programme.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Iran’s Mojtaba Khamenei urges Gulf rulers in written message to confront ‘real enemy’
articles.summary: Iran’s Supreme Leader ​Mojtaba Khamenei urged Muslim countries, particularly those in the Gulf, to unite against what he called their “real enemy” and said divisions among Muslims served the interests of their adversaries.
articles.body: Iran’s Supreme Leader ​Mojtaba Khamenei urged Muslim countries, particularly those in the Gulf, to unite against what he called their “real enemy” and said divisions among Muslims served the interests of their adversaries. The ⁠message was published on Khamenei’s Telegram account for Islamic Unity Week, which marks the birthday of the Prophet Muhammad. It called for Muslim unity, cooperation in various fields and mutual defence, saying anyone who ⁠creates divisions among Muslims, “knowingly or unknowingly,” ​helps ⁠Islam’s enemies. It asked whether Palestinians would have been left “so helpless” if Muslims had been united. Khamenei has not ⁠been seen in public since being injured in U.S.-Israeli airstrikes six ​months ⁠ago that launched the ‌Iran war, killing his father and previous supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. His call for unity echoes a statement he made ‌on Friday to Iranians, when he said ‌he had banned actions that harm social cohesion and urged authorities to avoid “discouraging statements” that weaken national and public morale. Khamenei specifically asked Gulf Arab rulers ⁠whether “rogues without identity” would have dared to covet their lands and possessions if the peoples and governments of the Gulf had been “united under the flag of Islam.” Since the 1979 Islamic Revolution, Gulf Arab monarchies have viewed Iran’s revolutionary ideology, including its anti-monarchic rhetoric and regional influence, as a threat to their ‌political systems. During the present conflict, Tehran has struck ​U.S. military facilities as well as other infrastructure in ‌Gulf states, underscoring the tensions ⁠between Tehran and its Gulf neighbours. “My emphatic and repeated recommendation ⁠to the rulers of Islamic countries, especially the countries of West Asia ‌and the Gulf, is ​to identify your real enemy, ‌understand his plan and confront it,” ​Khamenei said. War weighs on Iran’s economy Iranian leaders have acknowledged the economic toll of war with the U.S., with the supreme leader urging the government to ​address the hardship and the president saying foreign trade has shrunk by a third due to the American sanctions and blockade. Yet Tehran signalled no retreat on Saturday, ‌vowing to withstand U.S. pressure, pursue diplomacy and maintain what it said was control over the Strait of Hormuz, the strategic waterway giving Iran leverage through its ability to disrupt global energy markets. The government said in a statement on state media that addressing economic pressures caused by sanctions and war was a central focus, including curbing inflation, managing markets, creating jobs, directing investment towards domestic production and gradually reducing dependence on the dollar. Six months after the U.S. and ​Israel launched the war, negotiations are at an impasse and President Donald Trump’s administration has stepped up efforts to punish Iran financially with what it has billed as an “economic D-Day”. President Masoud Pezeshkian told state media that Iranian exports and imports had slumped nearly 35% because of U.S. sanctions and a naval blockade of Iranian ports. But he said Iran was able to sell about 90 million barrels of oil during the short-lived memorandum of understanding that the U.S. and Iran signed in June, when Washington permitted Iranian oil sales. Later on Saturday, Pezeshkian called on state TV for a revival of the interim deal, which was signed on June 17 but quickly unravelled amid disagreements over what had been agreed, especially ​on the status of the Strait of Hormuz. “We ​can solve our problems and gain our ⁠privileges with the memorandum of understanding,” he said of a document that had offered Iran, among other things, immediate relief from U.S. sanctions and the release of its frozen assets.

articles.title: Trump wants 'Lake America'. Canada puts up a 24-foot sign saying otherwise
articles.summary: US News: In a unique move, Doug Ford, premier of Canada's Ontario province, has put up a large banner along the shores of Lake Ontario, reading “Lake Ontario: .
articles.body: In a unique move, Doug Ford, premier of Canada's Ontario province, has put up a large banner along the shores of Lake Ontario, reading “Lake Ontario: Now and Always” in English and French.The move comes in response to US President Donald Trump’s recent decision to "rename" Lake Ontario as “Lake America”.In a video message, Ford described Lake Ontario as a “crown jewel” of both Ontario and Canada."You may have heard President Trump is trying to rename this lake, all because he doesn't like Ontario and Canada standing up for ourselves."Ford, however, asserted that Lake Ontario has always been known by that name and will continue to be called Lake Ontario."But, let's be serious. Long before President Trump, this lake was called Lake Ontario and long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario. But just in case President Trump or anyone else forgets, we've set up this sign to remind them - it's Lake Ontario now and forever," he added.Earlier, Trump signed an executive order directing the US Board on Geographic Names to refer to Lake Ontario as “Lake America”. While the executive order applies to American federal mapping agencies, it has no authority over Canadian territory or international hydrographic standards. Canadian leaders across party lines, along with US state officials, have largely dismissed or rejected the change.The order followed a similar move last year by the Trump administration to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the "Gulf of America."Lake Ontario is one of the five Great Lakes, which straddle the border between the two neighbouring countries.Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has already rejected Trump's "renaming" of Lake Ontario to “Lake America."US state officials, including New York governor Kathy Hochul, whose state borders the lake, said they would not adopt the new name, calling the move "absurd" amid pressing economic and trade concerns for agricultural exporters.Indigenous leaders, including Wendat Nation Grand Chief Pierre Picard, condemned the renaming as an "attempt to erase historical and cultural roots."(with ANI inputs)Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Zambian opposition leader Brian Mundubile charged with treason
articles.summary: Mundubile had previously gone into hiding at a United Nations building in Zambia's capital.
articles.body:
Zambian opposition leader Brian Mundubile has been charged with treason, his lawyer has said amid heightened political tensions in the country.

Mundubile was arrested on Thursday, after a deadly raid by the authorities led the opposition politician to go into hiding.

He had disputed the results of the country's recent presidential election, which saw incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema securing a second term.

The authorities then accused Mundubile's NRPUP party of planning an armed insurgency, which it denied.

On Saturday night, Mundubile's lawyer Milner Katolo announced that his client had been charged with treason. The opposition leader looks forward to answering the accusation in court, Katolo told the Zambian Eye .

The lawyer said 17 others, including Mundubile's running mate Makebi Zulu, had also been charged with treason.

Mundubile gained 38% of the vote in the 13 August election, while Hichilema secured 60%, official results show.

Following the raid, Mundubile and Zulu took refuge at a United Nations building in the city. The pair were detained after the president put pressure on the UN to hand them over.

The opposition was unable to mount a legal challenge to the election outcome as the courts were sealed off by the authorities on Monday, the final day that a case could be filed.

Hichilema is due to be sworn in for a second term on 1 September.

Regional and international observers described the election day as largely peaceful, but Zambia's Human Rights Commission has called for accountability over people whose whereabouts remain unknown following arrests and security operations around the elections.

articles.title: The home front: How Israel, Iran, and US leaders have been hit by the war
articles.summary: Six months into the US-Israel war on Iran, the governments in the three countries are fighting political wars at home.
articles.body:
Six months ago, the United States and Israel struck targets across Tehran, killing Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and other Iranian leaders.

It fulfilled a long-held ambition of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for a joint attack with the US on Iran, with Washington now locked in a war from which it is unable to extricate itself.

The US’s stated war aims also appear not to have been achieved, with President Donald Trump’s initial claim that Iran’s nuclear capacity had been destroyed now appearing false.

Netanyahu might have hoped that the fall of the government in Tehran would be part of his election campaign. And in Iran, the consequences of six months of war have done little to reverse the struggling economy, which appears to be the government’s Achilles heel.

The cost-of-living crisis was the mainstay of Trump’s criticisms of the previous administration of Joe Biden during the 2024 US election, but petrol prices alone have risen by 50 percent since the war on Iran began on February 28.

Trump’s repeated empty claims that a deal with Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz is imminent appear to be doing little to help his struggling Republican Party ahead of midterm elections due to take place in November .

Numerous surveys show Trump’s approval rating is at a record low, with criticism of his foreign policy competing with disapproval of his domestic record.

“The economic cost of the war is becoming a key issue for many,” Shibley Telhami, government and politics professor at the University of Maryland, told Al Jazeera.

Adding to the pressure on Trump are reports that he entered the unpopular war on Iran at the behest of Netanyahu, with fewer than one in three Americans supportive of the conflict, according to a recent Ipsos poll.

“There was a perception, certainly among Democrats but initially young Republicans, that this was a war that Israel had dragged the US into,” Telhami said. “The issue of Israel has risen in public priorities, as it is now not just a foreign policy issue but also a pocketbook and core values issue.”

In a bid to pile pressure on the Iranian government to agree to a deal that is more favourable to the US, Trump imposed new sanctions on Tehran last week, which he dubbed “Economic D-Day”.

Still, despite the costly effects of the war and sanctions on the Iranian economy and the destruction to its military, American author and diplomat Aaron David Miller pointed out that the government in Tehran has survived.

“The highly enriched uranium is still in the country and could still be enriched. Iran has also weaponised geography, in that it’s essentially closed off the Strait,” he told Al Jazeera.

“Likewise, their proxies in Hamas and Hezbollah, while much reduced, are still in place and still have capacity. The public unrest or internal dissent the US had hoped for hasn’t arisen. In terms of Iranian deterrence, it’s been a huge success for Tehran.”

The failure of Trump and Netanyahu’s military endeavour in Iran could have long-term effects on US foreign policy.

“No future administration is likely going to consider such a military campaign again,” said Miller.

Ahron Bregman, an Israeli security analyst and senior teaching fellow at King’s College London, said Netanyahu is viewed as having failed in Gaza, Lebanon and now in Iran. For Netanyahu, the war in Iran is perceived by many Israelis as a major security error.

“Netanyahu is trailing in the polls and for good reason,” Bregman said. “Instead of concentrating on stopping Iran from getting the bomb, he focused on – and convinced Trump to join him – regime change. It all failed, and Iran is now closer than ever to having the bomb.”

The US decision to sign a memorandum of understanding with Iran, without Israel’s involvement in June, provided Netanyahu’s political opponents with multiple reasons to attack the prime minister.

“I think Netanyahu was hoping this would be the electoral game-changer,” former Israeli government adviser Daniel Levy told Al Jazeera. “The war hasn’t gone as planned, so it hasn’t given him that momentum. If anything, it joins the list of things where he’s overpromised and underdelivered, given how much was expected of it as a decisive moment.”

The view that Iran still poses a fundamental threat to Israel, and the war has done nothing to minimise this, is a widely held belief among Israelis.

“I think [Netanyahu is] in favour of the economic ‘D-Day’ measures, not because he believes they’ll be decisive or that Iran will capitulate in talks, but because he’s hoping they’ll drive Trump’s frustration and put re-escalation back on the agenda, and that this time, things will look different,” Levy added.

Despite the Iranian government remaining in place, the sanctions and the US siege on Iranian ports do appear to be affecting the Iranian economy.

By Iran’s own reckoning, the war had already cost the economy upwards of $145bn by April, with annual inflation hitting 66 percent just last month. Taken in isolation, the US blockade could be inflicting $435m a day on the country. But the economy is still proving resilient to these challenges.

“I don’t want to downplay the effects of a crippled economy and of inflation, but my sense is that these pains remain manageable,” Shervin Malekzade, an academic and author on Iran, told Al Jazeera.

Iran’s entire political and military system was rooted in “the timeless task of preserving Iranian sovereignty and dignity against the world”, he added, helping it manage any economic challenges.

But there are still differences on economic issues within the Iranian government and a public rift between hardliners and moderates on the future of talks with the US.

Irrespective of the domestic political challenges thrown up by the war, none of the belligerents can concede defeat.

For Iran, the standoff with the US and Israel has gone beyond establishing deterrence and is a matter of survival.

Trump’s failure to deliver a short and decisive victory against Iran, and the economic and political costs of the war, will likely affect Republicans’ performance in the upcoming midterms.

For Israel, Iran remains no less of a perceived profound and existential threat than it did on February 27.

articles.title: Zelensky’s wonder-boy former defense minister goes rogue
articles.summary: Mykhailo Fedorov rocketed to prominence as a driving force in Ukraine’s pioneering use of drones in the fight against Russia, eventually becoming the country’s third defense minister of the war. Since being removed from that role last month, the wonder boy adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has taken a sharp turn against the administration…
articles.body:
Mykhailo Fedorov rocketed to prominence as a driving force in Ukraine’s pioneering use of drones in the fight against Russia, eventually becoming the country’s third defense minister of the war.

Since being removed from that role last month, the wonder boy adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has taken a sharp turn against the administration he long served, calling for elections and launching accusations of corruption and mismanagement.

Ukrainian lawmakers say the 35-year-old Fedorov seems to be trying to carve out a political lane separate from his longtime boss. But they worry he’s playing into Russia’s hands.

“During the war, things are very black and white — something that is helping us to win the war, and something that is the opposite, is not helping,” said Kira Rudik, a Ukrainian lawmaker with the opposition Holos party. “So, Fedorov was helping us to win the war for the last almost five years, and I think calling for the elections is the opposite, is not helping that.”

Fedorov’s call for new elections, in a video posted to YouTube last week, was the culmination of weeks of political intrigue and public outcry following his dismissal on July 15, after just six months on the job.

Thousands of protesters turned out across the country, calling for the minister’s reinstatement, with the biggest crowd gathering around the presidential office building in Kyiv. They also demanded that Zelensky fire Gen. Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander in chief of the armed forces, who had reportedly been feuding with Fedorov.

Zelensky sacked Syrskyi on July 21 but didn’t reverse his dismissal of Fedorov. During a meeting with reporters on Saturday, Zelensky said he offered Fedorov four other positions in the government, but he rejected all of them.

“I really had and still have a very positive attitude toward Mykhailo. We have been through a lot together. But I believe that he himself goes, or is pushed, into the wrong things,” Zelensky told reporters.

He argued holding elections amid the war “would be a tsunami for the state that would split Ukraine apart.”

Fedorov has only ramped up his criticism of the government in the past week, though he has avoided direct criticism of Zelensky.

After unsuccessfully running for Parliament soon after graduating from college, Fedorov became an adviser to Zelensky after his election in 2019, becoming minister of digital transformation. During a shake-up of the government in 2023, he became deputy prime minister for innovation, development of education, science and technology — a position he held until becoming defense minister in January 2026.

In media interviews over the past week, he has alleged that corruption involving hundreds of officials is holding back Ukraine’s war effort, and he decried entrenched patronage networks and poor military planning.

“I think that there’s now a turning point which will determine our future trajectory, but it looks as though we’re gradually, slowly losing,” Fedorov told Reuters this week.

His call for elections has been rejected across the political spectrum. Rudik asked why Fedorov was only speaking out when the possibility of his return to Zelensky’s Cabinet had closed.

“I think it was completely irresponsible of him,” she said, arguing that elections would be legally and logistically impossible, while pulling crucial resources away from the war effort.

“This is the Pandora’s box that he is pressing to be open. This is something that, at different times, President Trump demanded from Ukraine, but also something that Putin really wanted,” she added, referring to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

President Trump went as far as to call Zelensky a “dictator” during a breakdown in their relationship last year, echoing Russian talking points about the Ukrainian leader.

“He refuses to have Elections, is very low in Ukrainian Polls, and the only thing he was good at was playing Biden ‘like a fiddle,’” Trump said in a Truth Social post in February 2025.

Zelensky has mostly repaired his ties with Trump, though the U.S. has largely cut off support for Ukraine, contributing to its growing vulnerability to Russian missile and drone attacks.

Fedorov argues it’s his “moral right” to raise the issue of elections.

“That’s what democracy is all about. If I cannot share my ideas and be open about them with my own society, then what are we fighting for?” he told the BBC .

Oleksiy Goncharenko, a lawmaker with the European Solidarity party, isn’t buying it.

“I am in opposition to Zelensky. I think he’s a bad president, but it doesn’t change the fact that he is a legitimate president, and we can’t have elections because of security reasons, just physically,” he said.

“So when Fedorov calls for elections, what does it mean? So he puts his own personal political interest ahead of the country’s interest. It looks like this,” he added.

Goncharenko said Fedorov clearly had a base of support, as evidenced by the protests last month, but he had turned off some of his supporters with the call for elections.

While Fedorov’s political career is just getting started, Goncharenko said the first chapter was “not very promising.”

As the head of the Ukrainian Parliament’s temporary investigations commission, Goncharenko said he has summoned Fedorov for questioning on Monday over his claims of corruption.

“It’s a crime, especially during the war,” he said. “So, it’s not just that you think there are some mistakes, but now he speaks about corruption, which is crime, and which kills, literally, in the wartime.”

articles.title: Fears of more flooding in Nepal, 100 Americans among the missing as rescue efforts step up
articles.summary: KATHMANDU, Nepal — Authorities in Nepal have warned of the risk of further flooding after heavy rainfall, as China sheds light on the scale of the disaster in its Tibet region.
articles.body: KATHMANDU, Nepal — Authorities in Nepal have warned of the risk of further flooding after heavy rainfall, as China sheds light on the scale of the disaster in its Tibet region. Five days after surging floodwaters from a glacier collapse buried communities across the region in thick mud, rescuers in Nepal were still struggling to reach devastated communities as the full scale of the destruction emerged. “The disaster here is overwhelming,” Ferrin Cole, an operations director at the U.S.-based Crisis Response International, told NBC News on Sunday. “The flood that came down that mountain just wiped out cities. We’re going in as fast as we can to get people the help that they need.” Cole said his team would be working to help locate missing persons, but that working in mud “is actually pretty dangerous.” “The longer that death and mud are together, diseases breed, and so we’re always just aware of that,” he added. Approximately 100 Americans are among the missing across Nepal and China’s Tibet region, the State Department said Saturday. In Nepal, the death toll has risen to 781, with over 2,500 people still missing, including 592 foreign nationals, according to the country’s disaster agency. The Nepal Tourism Board said 289 foreign nationals have been rescued. China has separately reported 16 deaths and 546 people missing in its Tibet region, including 261 foreign nationals. It is unclear how much overlap there is between the Chinese and Nepali missing-person counts. Those missing loved ones may face a long wait for answers, with many bodies washed far downstream and recovered in poor condition. Morgues in Nepal have been overwhelmed, though authorities are collecting DNA samples in the hopes of notifying relatives. In Nepal’s Chitwan district, where a number of bodies have washed up, police officer Anil Thapa told Reuters that “more than half” of recovered bodies were “beyond recognition.” “Many have no visible faces. In some cases, only hands or legs remain,” the officer added. The response is also being complicated by a landslide-dammed lake above the border checkpoint that is overflowing, while heavy rain in Nepal has pushed up river levels and prompted fresh warnings for people living along waterways. Nepal’s flood alert system said Sunday that heavy rainfall had been measured in various watershed areas of Gandaki province, and that the water levels were “expected to rise.” “Therefore, people living in riverside areas are requested to adopt caution,” it said on X. But in flood-hit areas, residents were struggling to make sense of repeated warnings since the initial floods. “Sometimes they say a flood is coming, then we have to run again to higher ground, even at night. There is also rain,” Govind Shreshta, a resident of the town of Galchhi, told The Associated Press. “It’s really difficult for me. I have a 72-year-old father and 70-year-old mom. I must carry them and I am exhausted. It’s going on like this for those who are still alive.” Chinese state-run media outlet CCTV said Sunday that the event was part of a growing pattern of glacier-related disasters in the region, with the avalanche reaching China’s Gyirong Port within minutes of occurring. “The disaster was caused by glacier instability resulting from the long-term effects of climate warming,” said Chinese state media. “It struck suddenly, with a large peak flow, high speed, severe destructive force and a wide impact area,” the report added. “These are also new and significant characteristics of cryosphere-related disasters emerging across the Tibetan Plateau and surrounding regions.” While it will take time to determine the exact cause of the mudslide and flood disaster, analysts say climate change likely played a role. The Himalayan region, which includes Nepal, India, Pakistan, Bhutan, China and Afghanistan, is among the places most vulnerable to climate change, with temperatures rising faster than the global average. The warmer conditions are accelerating glacial melt, further destabilizing a region that is already prone to floods, landslides and earthquakes. The suspected collapse of a melting glacier shook the ground so violently that seismic monitors initially registered it as a magnitude-4.4 earthquake. The U.S. Geological Survey later revised that number to the equivalent of a magnitude-5.2 earthquake and said a second seismic event three hours after the first registered as the equivalent of a 4.2 temblor. Debris flow and flooding from what it called a “slope failure” traveled 62 miles, the USGS said. “We will not be able to attribute 100% that this is because of climate change, because these changes have been happening” over a long period of time, Neera Shrestha Pradhan, an expert at Nepal’s International Center for Integrated Mountain Development, said on Friday. But climate change might be breaking a threshold, she said, and “maybe that might be one of the causes of this happening.” Janis Mackey Frayer, Dawn Liu and Sunil Pandey reported from Kathmandu, Nepal. Freddie Clayton reported from London.

articles.title: At least seven dead and more missing after boat carrying hundreds capsizes off Cyprus
articles.summary: A rescue operation is underway in the Mediterranean after a passenger boat carrying nearly 270 people heading from Northern Cyprus to Turkey capsized, killing at least seven people.
articles.body: A rescue operation is underway in the Mediterranean after a passenger boat carrying nearly 270 people heading from Northern Cyprus to Turkey capsized, killing at least seven people. The Prime Minister of the Turkish republic of northern Cyprus, Ünal Üstel, told Turkish media that 237 people had been rescued from the ship, and search efforts were continuing for 23 people. Üstel said the ship capsized “due to the difficult weather conditions.” None of those rescued was in a critical condition. The Filo Jet was carrying 259 passengers and 8 crew members from Kyrenia to Taşucu in southern Turkey when it began taking on water just a few miles from the Cyprus coast, according to the Turkish Interior Ministry. Video from the scene of the ship’s capsizing showed dozens of people on the side of the vessel and others in life-jackets in the water. The speaker of the Turkish parliament Numan Kurtulmuş, said in post on X that he extended his condolences to those who had lost their lives in “this exceedingly tragic incident.” Four coastguard vessels from northern Cyprus and a passenger vessel took part in rescue operations, the Interior Ministry said, as well as two coastguard helicopters to the area. Video from the scene showed at least one helicopter hovering above the capsized vessel. The vessel was seen north of Kyrenia on Sunday morning, according to MarineTraffic tracking data, before transmissions of its position ceased. A live stream from Kyrenia showed people who had reached the port by helicopter and on rescue boats - amid the sound of ambulance sirens. Several ambulances were shown lined up at the harbor. Video of the capsized ship shows it on its side in choppy seas, with people wearing life jackets being picked up by rescuers and others in life jackets in the water. This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title: Israel’s Ben-Gvir lauds harsh conditions for Palestinian female prisoners
articles.summary: Palestinian groups condemn prison footage as humiliation and intimidation.
articles.body:
Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has posted footage from a prison holding Palestinian women on social media, boasting that he is responsible for the harsh conditions imposed on them.

The video, posted on Ben-Gvir’s X account on Sunday, shows him entering a section holding female prisoners and confronting them about their complaints regarding detention conditions.

One prisoner tells him: “This is our third day without showering. We are not receiving medical treatment, and our clothes are not clean.”

Ben-Gvir responds: “The good conditions in the prisons are over. This is the current situation, and I am directly responsible for everything. I am pleased with these conditions.”

In a post accompanying the video, the far-right minister wrote that the “whining” of prisoners over their conditions would not influence him, arguing that Israeli captives held in Gaza had not enjoyed adequate conditions.

“I’ll continue to lead a policy of the bare minimum of the minimum,” he said.

Gaza’s Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs condemned Ben-Gvir’s visit, saying the filming of female prisoners amounted to intimidation and humiliation.

It said his entry into the women’s section of the facility was “not an inspection visit”, but rather a “political spectacle and public incitement against the female prisoners” aimed at intimidating them and breaking their will in front of cameras.

The Palestinian agency said Ben-Gvir’s remarks showed that conditions inside Israeli prisons were part of what it described as a systematic policy of retaliation based on “humiliation, torture, starvation and deprivation”.

The Palestinian Prisoner’s Society also condemned the footage, telling Al Jazeera that Ben-Gvir’s filming and publication of the women constituted “an assault on their human dignity”.

It said hundreds of testimonies from released detainees and prisoners had documented serious abuses inside Israeli prisons and detention facilities.

Since becoming national security minister in late 2022, Ben-Gvir has pushed for tougher conditions for Palestinian prisoners, including reducing food and water supplies, restricting family visits, limiting shower times and removing privileges inside prison sections.

He has also overseen the transfer of hundreds of Palestinian prisoners between facilities.

Ben-Gvir has previously rejected efforts to improve conditions for prisoners. In 2025, he publicly opposed an Israeli court ruling requiring authorities to ensure Palestinian prisoners received adequate food, insisting that harsh conditions should continue.

According to the Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs, about 9,400 Palestinians are currently being held in Israeli prisons, including 88 women and more than 350 children.

articles.body:
President Trump this weekend announced a new deal for the U.S. to acquire majority control of over 65 million barrels of Venezuelan oil, which has prompted a mixed response on the home front.

Senate Democrats slammed the deal, describing the move as putting private profits over the safety of U.S. soldiers. GOP Sen. Bernie Moreno (Ohio) countered by saying it “benefits both countries for generations.”

Meanwhile, following Trump’s order to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America,” Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who has traded barbs with the president many times, is scheduled to appear on ABC’s “This Week” Sunday morning. Trump’s name change move came amid a trade war between the U.S. and Canada.

The president does not have an event on his Sunday public schedule.

articles.summary: Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodríguez on Saturday provided details on her country’s new oil deal with the U.S., after President Trump said much of Venezuela’s oil reserves will be under “majority U.S. control.” “This 25-year bilateral project envisages the development of 17 strategic oilfields with a production ​target of more than 1.5 million barrels per…
articles.body:
Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodríguez on Saturday provided details on her country’s new oil deal with the U.S., after President Trump said much of Venezuela’s oil reserves will be under “ majority U.S. control .”

“This 25-year bilateral project envisages the development of 17 strategic oilfields with a production ​target of more than 1.5 million barrels per day,” Rodríguez said on state TV outlet VTV in a late-night address. “That ⁠figure relates solely to the bilateral agreement between Venezuela and the United States.”

Rodríguez hailed the deal as “historic,” adding that it will revive Venezuela’s economy and increase government revenue.

“The agreement is based on a very simple premise,” she said. “Each party contributes what it does best. Venezuela contributes oil, its industry and the experience of its workers accumulated over more than 100 years. The United States contributes the capital and technology needed to recover and develop those assets.”

Rodríguez added that in return, “Venezuela receives production, jobs, investment in infrastructure, increased revenue for the government and productive linkages for domestic industry.”

The deal establishes $19 going to Venezuela for each barrel of oil produced and sold to the U.S., generating an estimated $209 billion a year to the South American country, she said. The benchmark price per barrel is $65, which she said could fluctuate based on global prices.

The $65 billion-per-barrel figure represents about 21 percent of Venezuela’s total proven reserves, which amount to 303 billion barrels.

Rodríguez noted that her country will own the natural resources “while leveraging capital, technology and operational expertise to support the recovery of a strategic industry that has been severely affected by sanctions.”

“But there is something that must be absolutely clear,” she said. “Venezuela retains ownership and sovereignty over its resources, while utilizing capital, technology and operational capacity to leverage the recovery of a strategic industry that has been severely hit by sanctions.”

Trump on Friday praised the deal as “THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY!” He wrote on Truth Social that the U.S. “secured majority U.S. control of more than 65 BILLION BARRELS of proven Oil Reserves in Venezuela, at no cost to the American Taxpayer.”

Rodríguez granted a joint venture between the U.S. government and a private operator in Venezuela 100-year “concessions” for oil fields containing 63 billion barrels of proven reserves, a U.S. official previously told The Hill.

Trump engaged with Venezuela over its oil following the U.S. capture of President Nicolás Maduro in January.

The push for oil production comes as the U.S. faces rising prices on energy amid the conflict with Iran, which has cut off oil exports from exiting the Strait of Hormuz, where roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil travels through.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) was among several Senate Democrats who pushed back on the deal , saying Friday that it “isn’t a win.”

“This is proof Trump put our service members at risk to get Venezuelan oil for his billionaire buddies,” he wrote on social media. “Putting our soldiers’ lives on the line for private profit is a gross dereliction of his constitutional duty.”

articles.title: Celebrity evangelist reflects on 2024 meeting with Hayden Panettiere after actress's sudden passing
articles.summary: Celebrity pastor Dylan Novak opened up about his 2024 encounter with Hayden Panettiere, revealing a "heartbreaking sadness" that hung over the late star.
articles.body: A Tennessee pastor who has shared the gospel with over 2,000 celebrities opened up about meeting actress Hayden Panettiere in 2024 following news of her untimely death on Aug. 16. Dylan Novak serves as a youth pastor at Henard's Chapel Missionary Baptist Church in Rogersville, Tennessee. He is also the founder of Celebrity Evangelist Ministries, a non-profit outreach dedicated to sharing the gospel with the world's most famous figures in what Novak calls a forgotten mission field. Novak recalled meeting Panettiere in April 2024 at Steel City Con in Monroeville, Pennsylvania, where he and his wife connected with the star over parenthood and raising daughters. While they were able to share their faith with the actress, Novak said he and his wife walked away feeling a heavy, "sad presence" surrounding Panettiere. "One thing my wife and I immediately started talking about after we met her was what a sad presence there was about her," Novak told Fox News Digital. "And I've talked a lot about that this past week. I wish we had had an opportunity to follow up with Hayden again." HAYDEN PANETTIERE REMEMBERED BY VIOLA DAVIS, BETHANY JOY LENZ AND OTHER CELEBRITIES AFTER SUDDEN DEATH AT 36 Novak added that people he said he knows in the entertainment industry who worked with Panettiere had shared similar observations. "I've talked with multiple people who I personally know who have worked with her, been around her, and all of them said pretty much the same thing," Novak said. "There was such a kindness about her, but there was also such a heartbreaking sadness that also surrounded her." Panettiere, who grew up on screen in films like "Remember the Titans" and "Ice Princess" before starring in the hit television dramas "Heroes" and "Nashville," was found unresponsive Aug. 16 at an apartment complex in Greenville, South Carolina. Preliminary autopsy results showed no signs of trauma that contributed to Panettiere’s death, according to the Greenville County Coroner's Office. Her death remains under investigation. Novak said he was saddened to learn of her passing and wished he'd had opportunities to speak with her again at other events, but he found comfort in knowing he'd had the chance to witness to her and give her faith resources. The news of her death reignited his belief in the urgency and importance of his ministry. "It just filled me with the fuel, the fire of the gospel of, we need to keep doing this. This is why we do what we do," he told Fox News Digital. "We all have the mindset when we see younger people... 'Oh, there'll be plenty of time. But really nobody knows except the Lord. That’s why it’s so important to make sure we continue to share that with everybody around us." Novak's ministry has reached over 2,000 celebrities with the gospel, including President Donald Trump, Tom Cruise, Keanu Reeves, Ozzy Osbourne, Jerry Lee Lewis and Sydney Sweeney. HAYDEN PANETTIERE DEFENDS GIVING UP CUSTODY OF HER DAUGHTER DESPITE INTENSE 'EMOTIONAL PAIN' He takes a personal approach to every encounter, telling each person he meets that he cares about them and where they are going after they die. Novak also brings customized gift bags with embossed Bibles, Christian resources and a handwritten note addressing specific comments the celebrity has made in interviews about faith and doubts. Over the years, those quiet conversations have borne surprising fruit. In 2023, Novak presented rock legend Ozzy Osbourne with a modern-translation Bible tailored to address Osbourne's difficulty understanding the Bible. Ozzy's son, Jack Osbourne, later told Novak his father kept the book on his nightstand and spent hours reading it. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Following Osbourne’s passing in July 2025, Novak says his ministry received hundreds of emails from fans asking for the same gospel resources he shared with Ozzy. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We had, no exaggeration, hundreds of people emailing us asking us for gospel information," Novak previously told Fox News Digital, noting that people were saying, "'Can you send me some of the material that you gave to Ozzy? I'm an old rocker, I rejected Christ years ago. But if Ozzy was willing to look at it, I'm willing to look at it.' People saying, ‘I want to be saved' and that is just so beautiful to see."

articles.title: Ford says Trump renaming Lake Ontario is ‘something out of Saturday Night Live’
articles.summary: Ontario Premier Doug Ford on Sunday said that President Trump’s executive order renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America” resembled “something out of ‘Saturday Night Live.’” Ford slammed Trump’s trade war with Canada that placed a 50 percent tariff on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods in an interview with “This Week” host Martha Raddatz on…
articles.body:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford on Sunday said that President Trump’s executive order renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America” resembled “something out of ‘Saturday Night Live.'”

Ford slammed Trump’s trade war with Canada that placed a 50 percent tariff on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods in an interview with “This Week” host Martha Raddatz on ABC.”

“I just don’t see the purpose. It’s absolutely backwards,” he said. “It was like something out of ‘Saturday Night Live’ when he signed a document saying ‘change to Lake America.’ No one’s going to call it Lake America. It’s been Lake Ontario for hundreds of years. It’s going to continue to be Lake Ontario.”

Ford called the tariffs and renaming “so, so disappointing, because I love the U.S. I love the American people. Canadians love the American people.”

“We differentiate between a great American people and the president,” he added.

Trump signed an executive order on Thursday to formally rename the Great Lake “effective immediately.” The president said that all “necessary papers, documents, everything else” were “filed.”

Trump had previously signed an executive order to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America.” The name change, appearing on Google Maps, led Mexico to file a lawsuit last year.

Lake Ontario appears on Google Maps named as “Lake America,” following Trump’s order.

“If you think about it, we have a gulf, now we have a lake, now all we need is an ocean,” Trump quipped. “Maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we’ll change them both.”

The Seneca Nation, one of the six nations of the Haudenosaunee, or Iroquois, Confederacy, on Friday called on Trump to rescind the order .

The nation’s president, J. Conrad Seneca, said the renaming violated the terms of the 1794 Treaty of Canandaigua , signed by leaders of the confederacy and President George Washington, which laid out the Seneca’s Nation’s boundaries as “beginning on Lake Ontario.”

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney dismissed the renaming , stating on Thursday that in the Wendat Nation’s language, “Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.”

“We know that America is changing,” Carney wrote on the social platform X. “Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always.”

Carney previously announced retaliatory tariffs on the U.S. beginning on Sept. 8. Seafood and fish products were exempt , but not copper wire, wood charcoal, steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics.

Though some lawmakers have criticized the tariffs , Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine) said the tariffs “ won’t go well ” for Canada.

“If Canada thinks they’re better off without our goods, I wish them good luck,” Golden told the Portland Press Herald on Tuesday. “I suspect in the long run, it won’t go well for them.”
